clue.text: Policeman getting stoned, in a dreadful state

parts.note: Detective Inspector, the usual crossword policeman
lapidation is the formal word for pelting someone with stones

explanation.surface: A police officer is high on drugs and in a sorry condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stoned' reads as drugged, but here it is the literal punishment by stones, LAPIDATION, from Latin lapis, a stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Dilapidation is ruin or disrepair, a building or thing gone badly downhill.

clue.text: Syrian's theatrical work missing right part of it?

parts.note: DRAMA without R, the abbreviation for right
a scene is one section of a play

explanation.surface: A question about a Syrian playwright's work that has lost part of its plot.
explanation.walkthrough: DRAMA SCENE with its first R dropped runs together as DAMASCENE; the question mark admits that 'part of it' leans on the drama just named.
explanation.definitionFit: Damascene means from Damascus, the capital city of Syria, so a native there is described by it.

clue.text: Exaltation and short satisfied expression for one in bed

parts.note: an exaltation is the collective noun for a flock of larks
PURR, a cat's contented sound, shortened by one letter

explanation.surface: A contented noise of joy from someone lying in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is a flower bed, not a place to sleep. 'Exaltation' is the rare collective name for larks, like a murder of crows.
explanation.definitionFit: Larkspur is a garden plant with tall spikes of blue flowers, grown in borders among other flowers.

clue.text: Old Brits, perhaps still way to the north

parts.note: a still is one kind of picture, PIC for short; 'perhaps' flags the example

indicators.note: in a down entry, heading north means reading upward, so the road abbreviation runs backwards

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Ancient Britons may still be found on the road heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' pretends to be an adverb meaning 'yet', but it is a noun: a single photograph from a film.
explanation.definitionFit: The Picts were an ancient people of northern Scotland, among the early inhabitants of Britain.

clue.text: Strike idiot in neck and face in scrap

indicators.note: the idiot sits in the middle of the neck-and-face pair, which wraps around it

parts.note: to neck a drink is to down it

indicators.note: the face of a word is its front, so only the first letter of 'scrap' is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of 'scrap'
tool is slang for a fool

explanation.surface: In a fight, someone punches a fool in the neck and face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neck' reads as a body part beside 'face', but it is the verb for swallowing a drink quickly, and 'face' is the front letter of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: To down tools is an idiom for workers stopping work in protest, which is what a strike does.

clue.text: Parent into Jack Kerouac at last — it's On The Road

indicators.note: the parent goes into the sailor, so the sailor's word wraps around it

parts.note: jack and tar are both old words for a sailor

indicators.note: at last means the final letter of the writer's surname is the only one used

parts.note: the final letter of Kerouac
mother, informally

explanation.surface: A parent gets into Jack Kerouac, author of the Beat novel On The Road.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Kerouac wrote On the Road, so the surface reads as one literary figure; in fact Jack is TAR, Kerouac supplies a single letter, and the title is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarmac is the tarred surfacing laid on streets, literally lying on top of any road.

clue.text: Animal that grazes in pen put up on island

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up means writing it bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: Biro is a brand name for a ballpoint pen
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A grazing beast is kept in a pen built on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The pen looks like an enclosure for the animal but is a writing pen; 'on' puts the reversed pen above the island letter in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The oribi is a small African antelope, a herbivore feeding on grass in savanna country.

clue.text: Idle, following extremely casual father

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the comedian's name is placed behind the two letters from 'casual'
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters of 'casual' are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of 'casual'
Eric Idle of Monty Python

explanation.surface: A lazy man trails behind his very relaxed dad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Idle' has a capital because it starts the clue, which hides that it is the surname of the Monty Python comedian, not an adjective meaning lazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Father is the title for a Catholic priest, and a priest is a member of the clergy.

clue.text: Struggle eating animal produce? Such a person would

indicators.note: a thing eating another has it inside, so the word for struggle surrounds the produce

parts.note: to vie is to compete or struggle
an egg is produced by a hen

explanation.surface: Someone struggles over whether to eat animal products, and the answer is a person who would.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the wordplay: a vegetarian, unlike a vegan, would happily eat animal produce such as eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Veggie is informal British for a vegetarian, who avoids meat but may eat dairy and hens' products.

clue.text: Hands clasping bird, one dwelling in trees

indicators.note: the two hands clasp the bird between them, one on each side

parts.note: left and right hands, L and R
the flightless Australian bird

explanation.surface: Someone holds a bird in their hands, a creature that lives up in the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' are not palms but the two sides, left and right, which close round EMU.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemur is a Madagascan primate that lives mostly among branches in the forest canopy.

clue.text: Fish cakes flipping green, with dessert being yellow

indicators.note: to cake something is to coat it thickly, so the fish forms a crust round the rest

parts.note: the common food fish

indicators.note: flipping a word turns it over, so the word for green runs backwards

parts.note: green means raw or inexperienced
an ice is a frozen dessert

explanation.surface: Fishcakes turning green, and the pudding going yellow: a kitchen disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish cakes' pretends to be a food, but cakes is a verb: the fish coats the reversed green. 'Yellow' is a colour in the surface and a character flaw in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow is slang for cowardly, so being yellow is showing a lack of courage.

clue.text: Opposes further exams head of school's introduced

indicators.note: something introduced is put inside, so the head letter goes into the exams

parts.note: resits are exams taken again after failing
the first letter of 'school'

explanation.surface: A headteacher opposes bringing in more exams.
explanation.walkthrough: The head of school is not a headteacher but just its first letter, slipped into RESITS after the I.
explanation.definitionFit: To resist is to stand against or fight back, a direct synonym of opposing something.

clue.text: Nearly trick chess champion, making exchanges

parts.note: TRAP, a trick, missing its final letter
Ding Liren, world chess champion 2023 to 2024

explanation.surface: Someone almost outwits a chess champion while swapping pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess picture suggests exchanging pieces, but the champion is a person: Ding Liren of China.
explanation.definitionFit: Trading is buying and selling, swapping goods or money back and forth.

clue.text: Means of buying audio version of The Unbearable Lightness of Being?

indicators.note: an audio version is heard rather than read, so the answer is what the description sounds like

parts.note: Milan Kundera's novel is a Czech book

explanation.surface: An audiobook of Kundera's famous novel, offered as a way to buy something.
explanation.walkthrough: The title is not wordplay fodder: you have to know the novel is by the Czech writer Milan Kundera. A cheque is the British spelling of check.
explanation.definitionFit: A chequebook holds bank cheques used to pay for goods, so it is a way to make purchases.

clue.text: Stole M Sartre's case in waterside shed

parts.note: a boa is a long scarf or stole
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a thou

indicators.note: a word's case is its outer shell, so only the outside letters of the philosopher's name are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of Sartre

explanation.surface: Someone stole Monsieur Sartre's suitcase from a shed by the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' is a noun, a scarf, not the past tense of steal, and 'M' is not Monsieur but a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: A boathouse is a building at the edge of a river or lake for storing boats.

clue.text: According to reporter, East End trio's at large

indicators.note: a reporter here is one who speaks, so the answer is the word as a Londoner would pronounce it

parts.note: in a Cockney accent of London's East End, th is often said as f

explanation.surface: A news report says three East End criminals are on the run.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney, the working-class accent of London's East End, turns th into f, so three is said 'free'.
explanation.definitionFit: At large describes an escaped prisoner not yet recaptured, so still loose and unconfined.

clue.text: Navy brought in new look for navy emblem

indicators.note: something brought in goes inside, so the navy letter enters the new look

parts.note: a redesign gives something a fresh appearance
N is the abbreviation for navy

explanation.surface: The Royal Navy commissions a rebrand of its badge.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Ensign is a British flag; strictly it belongs to the merchant navy rather than the Royal Navy, whose flag is the White Ensign.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign is a flag flown by ships, and this red one identifies British merchant vessels at sea.

clue.text: Fashion items around posh Hollywood area for model

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the posh letter and the Los Angeles letters
to fashion something is to shape it, so the letters of 'items' are reshaped

parts.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U speech
Hollywood is part of Los Angeles

explanation.surface: Designer clothes surround a posh Hollywood model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' and 'model' pull toward the catwalk, but fashion is the verb doing the shaping and model is a verb meaning imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: To model a system is to build a working imitation of it, just as a computer simulation does.

clue.text: Bishop abandons Italian riverbank

indicators.note: the bishop abandons the river, so its letter walks out of the name

parts.note: the river that runs through Rome
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
one printed word split across two jobs: its first half ends the wordplay, its second half is the definition

explanation.surface: A bishop walks away from an Italian riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riverbank' has to be split: 'Italian river' is the TIBER, and 'bank' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank can be a row or level of things one above another, like a tier of seats.

clue.text: T Rex oddly covering It Hurts Me — it's a hit!

indicators.note: the band's letters cover the cry of pain, one on each side
oddly means taking the letters in odd-numbered positions, first and third

parts.note: the first and third letters of T REX
what you say when something hurts you

explanation.surface: Glam rockers T. Rex release a cover version of a song called It Hurts Me, and it is a hit.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make 'It Hurts Me' look like a song title for T Rex to cover, but it is just the exclamation OUCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Touché is the fencer's call on being struck by an opponent's blade, conceding a scoring touch.

clue.text: One might get played in auditor's vile scam

indicators.note: an auditor is literally a listener, so the next word is taken as heard

parts.note: base means low or vile, and the low instrument word is said the same
a fiddle is a swindle

explanation.surface: Someone is taken for a ride in an accountant's nasty fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant checking the books, but it means a hearer, from Latin audire.
explanation.definitionFit: A bass fiddle is a double bass, a musical instrument, and instruments are what musicians play.

clue.text: Pupil hasn't started rewarding activity

indicators.note: not having started means the opening letter is missing

parts.note: a pupil is someone learning

explanation.surface: A student has not yet begun a worthwhile pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupil' could be the eye's pupil, but here it is a student, LEARNER, beheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: An earner, as in 'a nice little earner', is British slang for something that brings in money.

clue.text: New Yorker's behind acceptable British driver

parts.note: butt is American slang for the backside
as in 'that's not on', meaning not acceptable

explanation.surface: A New Yorker supports an agreeable British motorist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' reads as supporting, but it is the noun, the rear end, in American slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Jenson Button is the English racing driver who won the Formula One world championship in 2009.

clue.text: Storybook prefaced by a Spanish translator's intro

indicators.note: a preface comes at the front, so the Spanish article and the translator's letter go before the book

parts.note: un is Spanish for a

indicators.note: an intro is the start, so only the first letter of 'translator' is kept

parts.note: the first letter of translator
the Book of Ruth in the Old Testament
one printed word split across two jobs: its first half is the definition, its second half the book

explanation.surface: A children's storybook with a Spanish translator's introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Storybook' must be split: 'Story' is the definition and 'book' is a book of the Bible. 'Prefaced by' puts the other pieces in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A story can mean a lie, as when a child is told not to tell stories, and a lie is a falsehood.

clue.text: One might record duration of brief uprising

indicators.note: rising up in a down entry means reading from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: a remit is a brief, the scope of a task someone is given

explanation.surface: A historian might note how long a short-lived revolt lasted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective meaning short, but it is the noun, a set of instructions. 'Of' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A timer is a clock device that measures how long something takes, so it keeps note of elapsed time.

clue.text: Person in Black Sea abroad catches old vessel

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so the foreign sea holds the old vessel

parts.note: mer is French for sea
O is the abbreviation for old
an urn is a vase or container

explanation.surface: Someone on the Black Sea overseas catches sight of an ancient ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black Sea' reads as the Eurasian sea, but 'Black' ends the definition and 'Sea abroad' starts the wordplay. The vessel is a pot, not a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Mourners at a funeral traditionally wear dark clothes as a sign of grief.

clue.text: Enchanting person's publication — the Guardian?

parts.note: short for magazine
the setter's newspaper speaking of itself

explanation.surface: A charming person's writing appears in the Guardian newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle appeared in the Guardian, so 'the Guardian' refers to the paper itself: US, just as 'this writer' gives ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A magus is a sorcerer or wise man, one who casts spells, which is enchanting in its old sense.

clue.text: Luvvie, attacked by bee crossing river, hobbled

parts.note: a ham is an overacting actor; luvvie is British slang for a gushing theatrical type

indicators.note: the bee's attack is crossing the river, lying across it on both sides

parts.note: what a bee does to you
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: An actor stung by a bee as he crossed a river went limping away.
explanation.walkthrough: A luvvie is a British mocking word for an actor, especially a showy one; HAM is the crossword actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamstrung means crippled or severely restricted, originally by cutting the tendons at the back of the knee.

clue.text: American, as it happens, is quick

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
describes a broadcast going out in real time rather than recorded

explanation.surface: Americans, as it turns out, are fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' means fast in the surface, but here it is the old sense found in 'the quick and the dead'.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick in its archaic meaning is living, as in the biblical phrase about judging the living and dead.

clue.text: Outspoken genius rejects one scientist playing God

parts.note: frank means blunt and candid
EINSTEIN, the byword for genius, without I, the Roman one

explanation.surface: A blunt genius turns away a scientist who thinks he is God.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scientist' looks like part of the wordplay beside 'genius', but it belongs to the definition, which runs to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Frankenstein in Mary Shelley's novel creates life, usurping a power reserved for the Creator.
